I’ve been thinking lately about the way light changes through a window in the late afternoon—how it starts out bold and golden, almost arrogant in its warmth, and then slowly surrenders to something softer, more uncertain, before it disappears. There’s something honest about that transition. It doesn’t cling.

We live in a time that feels obsessed with permanence. We archive everything. We backup our backups. We panic at the thought of a message disappearing, a photo lost, a moment unrecorded. And yet, the things that actually stay with us are often the ones we never captured—the smell of rain on hot asphalt, the way someone’s voice cracked when they said something vulnerable, the specific silence of a room after a difficult conversation. Memory is imperfect, and maybe that’s its power. It edits. It curates. It keeps what mattered and lets the rest dissolve, like the afternoon light.

I’ve also been thinking about hands. How we use them to gesture when we’re trying to explain something we don’t fully understand ourselves. How they age faster than the rest of us, telling stories we might not be ready to tell. How a pianist’s hands look different from a carpenter’s, not just in wear but in intention, in what they’ve been trained to expect from the world.

There’s a kind of writing I admire that doesn’t rush to a point. It meanders, trusts the reader, assumes intelligence without needing to prove its own. I suppose that’s what I’m trying to do here—not deliver a thesis, but think alongside you. Because thinking is often lonely, and the best conversations I’ve had weren’t debates but mutual wanderings, two people holding flashlights in adjacent dark rooms, occasionally calling out what they see.

Anyway. The light is gone now. The window is just glass again, reflecting the lamp behind me. But for a while, it was something else entirely. That’s enough.
